claims.text: Social media use has a very small linear association with depression outcomes in young people (pooled r = .08, 95% CI [0.04, 0.11]).
Social media use has a very small linear association with anxiety outcomes in young people (pooled r = 0.093, 95% CI [0.059, 0.126]).
Year of publication does not moderate the effect of social media use on depression outcomes.
Duration of follow-up does not moderate the effect of social media use on depression outcomes.
Mean age of sample does not moderate the effect of social media use on depression outcomes.
Social media use is unlikely to account for the contemporary youth mental health crisis.

evidence.description: Meta-analysis of twelve studies examining depression outcomes found pooled r = .08, 95% CIs [0.04, 0.11], showing very small linear effects.
Meta-analysis of five studies examining anxiety outcomes found pooled r = 0.093, 95% CIs [0.059, 0.126], showing very small linear effects.
Moderator analysis showed no moderating effects for year of publication for the depression effects.
Moderator analysis showed no moderating effects for duration of follow-up for the depression effects.
Moderator analysis showed no moderating effects for mean age of sample for the depression effects.
Conclusions drawn from the identified very weak relationships between social media use and severity of anxiety and depression symptoms.

methodologies.name: Systematic review and meta-analysis
methodologies.description: Systematic search across PsycINFO, Web of Science, MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus to meta-analyze longitudinal and experimental studies on social media use and youth anxiety and depression.
conditions: Social media use measured by time or frequency
Standardized measures of depression and anxiety

limitations.text: Included studies measured social media use mainly via self-report.
The eligible literature contained almost exclusively longitudinal observational studies (36 studies) and only one experimental study.

future_work.text: Conduct longitudinal research designed to examine potential non-monotonic relationships between social media use and adverse mental health outcomes.
Investigate other potential causes of increased prevalence of mental health problems in young people.
